questions.q: Is Thistledown Retail Group, the company in this case study, a real business?
options: No — it's explicitly described as a fictional, illustrative composite scenario
Yes — it is a real, named retail company
Yes — it is a real company whose name was changed for privacy
The lesson does not say whether it is real or fictional
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly labels Thistledown Retail Group as fictional and illustrative, consistent with this catalog's policy against presenting invented scenarios as real.

questions.q: What was the root problem at Thistledown Retail Group before the Purview rollout?
options: Four regions each kept their own spreadsheet definitions, with no shared catalog or picture of what data existed
The company had no computers at all
All data was already perfectly governed and the rollout was unnecessary
The company had too many Purview accounts and needed to delete some
questions.explain: Each region maintained its own definitions and systems with no shared catalog, so nobody at the corporate level could say what data existed, where it lived, or who could see it.

questions.q: In the Chapter 2 step of the rollout, what specifically caused one region's Data Map scan to stall?
options: A storage firewall rule blocking Purview's managed identity
The data source admin role didn't exist yet in Purview
The scan rule set was deleted entirely
Azure Data Lake Storage doesn't support scanning
questions.explain: The scan troubleshooting in the case study traced the stall to a storage firewall rule blocking the scan's managed identity — a concrete, specific cause rather than a vague issue.

questions.q: What did Chapter 4's catalog and glossary work replace at Thistledown Retail Group?
options: Four competing regional definitions of 'SKU' with one glossary-defined term and an accountable steward
The company's entire Azure subscription
All four regional distribution centers with a single warehouse
The need for any data source to ever be scanned
questions.explain: Rather than four separate definitions, the team published one glossary term for SKU (and for In-Stock Quantity) with a clear definition and steward, used consistently across all regions.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why did the rollout work six months later?
options: The rollout touched every layer the course covered, in the order the course taught them — foundations, then data, then meaning, then trustworthy use
The company hired an entirely new IT department from scratch
All four regional systems were simply deleted with no replacement
Executives stopped looking at the Power BI reports entirely
questions.explain: The case study's closing point is that the rollout's success came from applying every chapter's concepts in sequence — foundations first, then the Data Map, then classification, cataloging, lineage, and governance workflows — not from a single fix.
